summary: Describes plans for a longitudinal measurement study of changes in service-level reachability in the global TCP/IP Internet. It covers the goals, experimental design, implementation and policy considerations. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Scientists planned to check over time which services on the Internet could be reached, and wrote down the plan.

questions: how to measure internet service reachability
subtitle: A longitudinal study tracking which Internet services sites are willing to run.

tldr.problem: The Internet is growing and becoming more security-conscious, but it is not clear how these security measures are changing the services sites offer to the network.
tldr.mechanism: Researchers designed a systematic measurement study to probe 13 common TCP services at approximately 12,700 Internet domains over one year, running bimonthly to track trends.
tldr.outcome: The study provides baseline data about Internet service reachability evolution, including how geographic location and institution type affect service availability and willingness to participate in inter-organizational computing.

facts.label: Network load from study
facts.value: less than 0.5% of NSFNET backbone traffic

today: RFC 1273 is an Informational RFC that describes the design of an Internet measurement study. It remains historically significant as an early example of systematic Internet-wide measurement methodology and the ethical considerations involved in conducting such studies.

sections.title: The Problem Being Studied
sections.content:
The global TCP/IP Internet connects millions of people, but this open connectivity creates security risks. Many sites have responded by limiting services they offer—disabling certain services, using gateways that only allow email, or disconnecting entirely. This study measures whether these security decisions are reducing Internet service availability over time.

Instead of measuring basic IP connectivity, the researchers focus on service-level reachability—whether application services like FTP, telnet, and domain naming are actually available. This matters because it shows the willingness of organizations to support distributed computing and collaboration.
sections.plainLanguage: When people worry about computer security, they sometimes unplug services or lock down their network. This study checks if that is really happening across the whole Internet.

sections.title: How the Study Works
sections.content:
The measurement study runs over one year with six rounds, occurring bimonthly (January, March, May, July, September, November 1992). Each round takes one to two days. The software attempts to connect to 13 different TCP services at approximately 12,700 Internet domains worldwide and records whether each connection succeeds or fails.

The 13 services tested are: daytime, netstat, FTP, telnet, SMTP, Domain Name Service, finger, Sun portmap, rlogin, rsh, UUCP, klogin, and krcmd/kshell. These services represent a range of common uses. No actual data is transferred—connections are simply opened and closed, so security mechanisms are not tested.
sections.plainLanguage: Six times over a year, the study tried to say hello to 13 different services on almost 13,000 computers, and kept score of what answered back.

sections.title: Controlling Load and Impact
sections.content:
The measurement software is carefully designed to avoid generating unnecessary Internet traffic. Once a connection to a service succeeds in a domain, the software never tries that service on other machines in that domain during the current measurement run. After 3 connection refusals at a domain, it stops trying that service there. After 3 timeouts on any machine in a domain, it gives up on the entire domain for that run.

Test runs in August 1991 show the study is very lightweight: 50,549 domain lookups and 73,760 connection attempts completed in 10 hours, generating less than 0.5% of NSFNET backbone traffic that day. The cost to remote sites being measured is effectively zero—on average only 5.7 connections per domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The study is designed to be polite to the Internet: it stops trying things that do not work, and it does not use much network traffic or bother remote computers.

sections.title: Privacy and Ethical Concerns
sections.content:
Measuring network services raises privacy and security concerns. The researchers initially tried to notify site administrators via email and USENET, but discovered that announcement messages themselves created more network load than the study. Announcing the study also risked biasing results, as sites might change their reachability specifically in response to being notified.

Instead, the researchers published this RFC as advance notice and identified themselves through a special login account called 'testnet' that returns information about the study via the finger protocol. The raw data is treated as sensitive and results are published only as global statistics, never tied to individual sites.
sections.plainLanguage: The researchers had to decide when and how to tell sites they were being measured. Too much warning would change the results. So they published their plan ahead of time and identified themselves if anyone asked.

sections.title: What This Study Reveals
sections.content:
The measurement data will show which mechanisms sites use to distance themselves from full Internet participation, which services organizations are willing to run, and how these choices vary by geographic location and institution type (commercial, educational, government). These trends help application designers and network builders understand what distributed applications are feasible to deploy.

The study contributes to understanding Internet evolution at a societal level—directly measuring how a global electronic society is developing and adapting to security concerns.
sections.plainLanguage: By learning which services are available where, scientists can figure out what kinds of new applications people will actually be able to use across the Internet.
